concepts.def: The low-level ionising radiation that is around us all of the time. It comes from natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space, and from man-made sources such as the fallout from nuclear weapons testing and nuclear accidents.

Sources that are not produced by human activity, such as rocks and cosmic rays from space. Rocks in the ground and in building materials contain radioactive isotopes, so a low level of radiation is always present.

Ionising radiation that reaches the Earth from space. The atmosphere absorbs a large part of it, so the dose received from cosmic rays is greater at high altitude, where there is less atmosphere above you.
Sources that exist because of human activity. The specification gives the fallout from nuclear weapons testing and from nuclear accidents as the examples.
Radioactive material thrown into the atmosphere by a nuclear weapons test or a nuclear accident, which then spreads and settles onto land and water, adding to the background radiation there.

concepts.term: Effect of occupation on radiation dose
concepts.def: The radiation dose a person receives may be affected by the job they do. People who work with radioactive sources or with radiation-producing equipment, such as radiographers and workers in the nuclear industry, may receive a higher dose than the rest of the population, so their dose is monitored.

concepts.term: Effect of location on radiation dose
concepts.def: The level of background radiation may be affected by where a person is. Places built on rock types that contain more radioactive isotopes have a higher background level, and places at high altitude receive a larger dose from cosmic rays.

A measure of the risk of harm to the body resulting from exposure to ionising radiation. Radiation dose is measured in sieverts (Sv). It is not the same as activity, which counts the decays per second in a source.

The sievert (Sv) is the unit of radiation dose. Everyday doses are small, so they are usually quoted in millisieverts: 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). To convert a dose in mSv to Sv, divide by 1000.
Radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values, from small fractions of a second for some isotopes to thousands of millions of years for others.

For a given number of undecayed nuclei, a short half-life means many decays happen each second, so the activity is high and the radiation emitted is intense. The hazard is severe but short-lived, because the activity falls away quickly.

For a given number of undecayed nuclei, a long half-life means fewer decays each second, so the activity is lower. The hazard is less intense but lasts far longer, because the material stays radioactive for many years, so contamination of land, water or a workplace remains a problem for a very long time.

A use of nuclear radiation in medicine in which a small amount of a radioactive isotope is swallowed, injected or inhaled. The radiation it emits passes out of the body and is detected outside, so doctors can follow where the substance goes and see how an organ is working, without surgery.

concepts.term: Control or destruction of unwanted tissue (radiotherapy)
concepts.def: A use of nuclear radiation in medicine in which radiation is directed at unwanted tissue, such as a tumour, to control its growth or destroy it. The dose is concentrated on the tumour, but healthy tissue nearby still receives some radiation.

concepts.term: Evaluating a use of nuclear radiation
concepts.def: Judging a use by setting its benefits against its drawbacks: the information a scan gives or the tissue a treatment destroys, weighed against the dose received, the possible damage to healthy cells and the alternatives available.

The risk people believe a use of nuclear radiation carries is often different from the risk shown by data on doses and consequences. An evaluation must use the data given — for example comparing a dose with the background dose received anyway — rather than the strength of feeling about radiation.

concepts.term: Choosing an isotope for a medical use
concepts.def: The half-life and the type of radiation determine how hazardous an isotope is and what it can be used for. A tracer needs a half-life long enough for the scan but short enough that the activity falls quickly afterwards, and radiation penetrating enough to leave the body and reach a detector.

mcqs.q: Which statement about background radiation is correct?
options: It is around us all of the time, from natural and man-made sources.
It is only present in places affected by a nuclear accident.
It exists only because humans have used nuclear technology.
It is only found in places where uranium-bearing rocks occur.
mcqs.explain: Background radiation is continuously present and has both natural sources, such as rocks and cosmic rays from space, and man-made sources, such as fallout.

mcqs.q: Which of these sources of background radiation is a natural source?
options: Fallout left by nuclear weapons testing
Cosmic rays arriving from outer space
Emissions released in a nuclear accident
Fuel rods used in a nuclear reactor core
mcqs.explain: The specification names cosmic rays from space, alongside rocks, as an example of a natural source of background radiation.

mcqs.q: People who live high up a mountain receive a larger radiation dose from cosmic rays than people at sea level. Why?
options: They are further from the radioactive rocks in the ground.
Cosmic rays are produced by the thinner air found high up.
There is less atmosphere above them to absorb the cosmic rays.
They are closer to the Sun, the only source of cosmic rays.
mcqs.explain: Cosmic rays come from space and are absorbed as they pass through the atmosphere, so less overhead atmosphere means a greater dose.

mcqs.q: Which pair are both man-made sources of background radiation?
options: Fallout from weapons testing and cosmic rays
Rocks in the ground and fallout from nuclear accidents
Cosmic rays from space and rocks in the ground
Fallout from weapons testing and nuclear accidents
mcqs.explain: These are exactly the two examples of man-made sources given by the specification.

mcqs.q: A radiographer wears a badge at work that records the radiation dose she receives, and her total dose each year is checked. Which statement best explains why this is done?
options: Everyone receives the same dose, so all workers are checked.
Her occupation can raise the radiation dose she receives.
The badge lowers the dose the radiographer receives at work.
The badge measures the activity of the sources in becquerels.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that radiation dose may be affected by occupation; working with radiation-producing equipment can raise her dose above that of the general population.

mcqs.q: Two identical houses are built in different parts of the country, one on granite and one on clay. Which statement about the background radiation in the two houses is correct?
options: Both houses have exactly the same background level.
The clay house has more because clay is denser rock.
Neither house has any, since rocks are not radioactive.
Background level can differ because the rocks differ.
mcqs.explain: Rocks are a natural source of background radiation and different rock types contain different amounts of radioactive isotopes, so location affects the level.

mcqs.q: A worker's radiation dose for one year is recorded as 3.6 millisieverts (mSv). What does this dose tell you?
options: The risk of harm from the radiation received.
The number of decays each second in the source.
The energy stored in the radioactive source used.
The mass of radioactive material absorbed.
mcqs.explain: Radiation dose, measured in sieverts, is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from the body being exposed to ionising radiation.

mcqs.q: A patient receives a radiation dose of 4.5 mSv. Given that 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), what is this dose in sieverts?
options: 45 Sv

mcqs.q: In one year worker P receives a dose of 0.8 mSv and worker Q receives a dose of 0.0015 Sv. Use 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). Which comparison is correct?
options: P receives the higher dose, as 0.8 is the larger number.
The two doses are equal once the units are converted.
Q receives the higher dose, about 1000 times that of P.
Q receives the higher dose, about twice that of P.
mcqs.explain: 0.0015 Sv = 1.5 mSv, and 1.5 mSv is a little under twice 0.8 mSv, so Q receives roughly double P's dose.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the half-lives of radioactive isotopes is correct?
options: They are all of a similar length, around a few years.
The most hazardous isotopes always have the longest ones.
They range from fractions of a second to billions of years.
Every isotope of a given element has the same half-life.
mcqs.explain: Radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values, which is why the hazards they present differ so greatly.

mcqs.q: Two sealed sources contain the same number of undecayed nuclei. Source X has a half-life of 8 days and source Y has a half-life of 1600 years. Which statement is correct?
options: X gives the higher activity now, but for a shorter time.
Y is more hazardous now because its half-life is longer.
X is completely harmless because it decays away fast.
Y decays faster now, so it releases more radiation today.
mcqs.explain: With equal numbers of nuclei, the shorter half-life means more decays each second now, so X is more intense but its activity falls away quickly.

mcqs.q: Radioactive material is spilled on a laboratory floor. Why is a spill of an isotope with a half-life of 30 years a longer-term problem than a spill of one with a half-life of 6 hours?
options: The 30-year isotope emits far more radiation each second.
A spill of the 6-hour isotope emits no radiation at all.
Half-life does not affect how long contamination lasts.
It stays significantly radioactive for many decades.
mcqs.explain: A 30-year half-life means the activity halves only once in 30 years, so the contaminated area remains hazardous for a human lifetime, while the 6-hour isotope decays to a low activity within days.

mcqs.q: A patient is given a small amount of a radioactive substance so that doctors can follow where it goes inside the body. This is an example of:
options: exploring internal organs with nuclear radiation
destroying unwanted tissue with nuclear radiation
reducing the patient's background radiation dose
making the patient permanently radioactive
mcqs.explain: This is the use the specification calls the exploration of internal organs: a tracer whose radiation escapes the body and is detected outside.

mcqs.q: Which combination of properties makes an isotope suitable for use as a medical tracer?
options: It emits alpha radiation, which is strongly ionising.
It has a very long half-life so it lasts in storage.
It emits gamma radiation and has a short half-life.
It stays at the same activity for the whole of a scan.
mcqs.explain: Gamma radiation is penetrating enough to escape the body and reach a detector, and a short half-life means the activity falls quickly once the scan is over.

mcqs.q: During radiotherapy, gamma radiation is aimed at a tumour from several different directions. Which statement best explains why?
options: Healthy tissue is not affected by gamma radiation at all.
The tumour gets a high dose while healthy tissue gets less.
Gamma radiation only damages cells where beams overlap.
It makes the treatment completely free of any risk.
mcqs.explain: Every beam passes through the tumour but each takes a different path through healthy tissue, so the dose concentrates on the tumour.

mcqs.q: A doctor must decide whether to use a radioactive tracer scan on a patient. Which approach is the best way to evaluate this use of nuclear radiation?
options: Refuse it, because every use of radiation carries a risk.
Weigh the dose received against the benefit of a diagnosis.
Accept it, because medical scans are always safe for patients.
Compare the activity in becquerels with the legal limit.
mcqs.explain: Evaluating means setting the measured drawback, the dose and its risk, against the benefit, the information the scan gives about the patient's illness.

mcqs.q: A hospital leaflet states that a chest scan gives a dose of about 0.1 mSv, and that the average dose from background radiation in the UK is about 2.7 mSv per year. Which conclusion do these data best support?
options: The scan should be refused because any dose is harmful.
The scan adds much less than a year of background dose.
Background dose is the same for everyone, so this is exact.
The scan gives about 27 times the yearly background dose.
mcqs.explain: 0.1 mSv is about one twenty-seventh of 2.7 mSv, so the extra dose is a small fraction of what the patient receives from background radiation anyway.

mcqs.q: Radiotherapy to destroy a tumour also carries a risk of damaging healthy cells. Which statement is the best evaluation of that risk?
options: The risk is smaller than that of leaving the cancer.
Radiotherapy should never be offered to any patient.
There is no risk, since beams reach only the tumour.
The risk cannot be judged unless the dose is zero.
mcqs.explain: Evaluating a perceived risk means comparing consequences: damage to some healthy cells is set against the consequences of an untreated tumour.
